metadata.source: Dravyaguna Vijñāna (Dravya_guna3_med_p2.pdf) — Appendix: Therapeutic (Disease-Wise) Indication of Drugs
metadata.notes: Continuation batch 3. Covers O–P diseases. Botanical names cross-referenced with standard Ayurvedic pharmacognosy.

diseases.description: Excessive accumulation of body fat causing increased body weight and associated metabolic disorders. In Ayurveda, medoroga arises from vitiated kapha and meda dhātu (fat tissue), weak digestive fire, and sedentary lifestyle. One of the eight body types (aṣṭa nindita) considered unfavourable.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Useful in slimming or reducing body (weight)
Anti-obese; anti-obesity; anti-fat or reducing fat (medohara)
Promoting fat (herbs to avoid in obesity)

diseases.description: General category for complications during pregnancy and childbirth including miscarriage, difficult labour, placenta retention, and post-partum fever. Ayurveda devotes an entire branch (Kaumāra bhṛtya / Prasūtitantra) to obstetric management.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Alleviating disorders of female genital organs

diseases.description: Spontaneous loss of pregnancy before 20 weeks. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated vāta, pitta, or kapha affecting the garbha (foetus) and garbhāśaya (uterus). Herbs that stabilise the foetus and support the uterus are prescribed.

herbs.name: Nyagrodhādi gaṇa
herbs.botanical: Group of five fig trees (Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Asvattha, Plaksha, Madhuka)

diseases.description: Swelling caused by excess fluid trapped in the body's tissues. Can be localised or generalised (anasarca). In Ayurveda, śotha is caused by vitiated vāta, pitta, or kapha, or by weak digestive fire producing āma that blocks the channels. Six types described based on doṣa involvement.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Removing, pacifying, decreasing and alleviating kapha

diseases.description: Discharge of pus from the ear — indicating chronic suppurative otitis media. In Ayurveda caused by kapha accumulation and kṛmi (microbial) infection in the ear canal and middle ear.

Pain occurring after digestion of food — characteristic of peptic ulcer and duodenal ulcer. The pain worsens after meals as food stimulates acid secretion. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated pitta and vāta in the āmāśaya (stomach/duodenum).

Diseases specific to children — including bālagraha (childhood infections), nutritional deficiencies, teething disorders, skin problems, and respiratory conditions. Kaumāra bhṛtya is a dedicated branch of the eight limbs of Ayurveda.

Swollen and inflamed veins in the rectum and anus causing discomfort, itching, and bleeding. In Ayurveda, arśa is caused by vitiated tridoṣa, poor diet, and sedentary habits. Classified as dry (śuṣka) or bleeding (srava), and as internal or external. One of the eight major diseases in classical Ayurveda.

herbs.name: Pañcakola
herbs.botanical: Group: Pippali, Pippalimula, Cavya, Citraka, Sunthi

diseases.description: Inflammatory skin papules and pustules (acne). In Ayurveda caused by vitiated pitta and kapha blocking the svedavaha srotas (sweat channels) of the face and body. Aggravated by oily food, stress, and hormonal changes.

Retention of the placenta after childbirth — a serious obstetric emergency. In Ayurveda, herbs are prescribed to stimulate uterine contraction and facilitate expulsion of the retained placenta (aparā).

General category for poisoning — from animal, plant, mineral, or artificial sources. In Ayurveda viṣa (poison) is classified as sthāvara (plant/mineral), jāṅgama (animal), and kṛtrima (artificial). The branch of Agada tantra specialises in toxicology and antidotes.

Toxicity from artificially prepared poisons — including adulterated food, compound toxins, and chemically induced poisoning. In Ayurveda's Agada tantra, specific antidotes are prescribed for different poison preparations.
Toxic reaction to bee or wasp stings causing local swelling, pain, and potentially systemic anaphylaxis. In Ayurveda treated with specific antidotes that neutralise the venom.
Toxic reactions to insect bites and stings — from beetles, centipedes, scorpions, and other insects. In Ayurveda each type of insect poison has specific characteristics and antidotes.

Viral encephalitis transmitted through animal bites — especially dogs. In Ayurveda classified as a type of animal-origin poison (jāṅgama viṣa) from dog bites (śvadaṁśa). Associated with intense fear, hydrophobia, and neurological symptoms.
Venomous sting from scorpions causing intense local pain, swelling, and systemic effects including neurological symptoms, hypertension, and cardiac complications in severe cases.

Venomous snakebite causing local tissue damage, systemic effects including coagulopathy, neurotoxicity, or haemotoxicity depending on the species. In Ayurveda sarpāghāta (snakebite) has specific management protocols in Agada tantra, with detailed classification of snake species and their venoms.
Toxic reactions to spider bites — causing local tissue damage, pain, and systemic effects. In Ayurveda lūtā (spider) poisoning has specific presentations and antidotes described in Agada tantra.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Counteracting spider-poisoning; alleviating wound caused by spider

diseases.description: Smallpox and chickenpox — vesicular eruptions with fever, body ache, and characteristic skin lesions progressing from macules to papules, vesicles, pustules, and scabs. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated rakta, pitta, and kapha with specific bīja (infective agent) involvement.

Combined white and red vaginal discharge — indicating both kapha and pitta/rakta vitiation in the yonimārga. Encompasses a spectrum from leucorrhoea (śveta) to menorrhagia (rakta) and mixed presentations.

herbs.name: Candana (dvaya)
herbs.botanical: Santalum album Linn. & Pterocarpus santalinus Linn. f.

diseases.description: Swelling of limbs and face during pregnancy due to fluid retention. Physiological swelling is normal in late pregnancy, but pathological oedema indicates gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia.
Abdominal and pelvic pain during pregnancy. Can be round ligament pain, uterine cramping, or early labour pains. Requires gentle, pregnancy-safe analgesic and antispasmodic herbs.

A group of 20 urinary disorders characterised by turbid, copious, or abnormally coloured urine. Includes glycosuria, phosphaturia, albuminuria, and related metabolic disorders. Prameha is considered a precursor to madhumeha (diabetes). Caused by vitiated kapha obstructing mūtravaha srotas and impairing metabolism.

herbs.name: Śālasārādi gaṇa
herbs.botanical: Group including Sal and related trees

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Anti-diabetic; alleviating prameha group of diseases, esp. madhumeha
Removing, pacifying, decreasing and alleviating kapha

diseases.description: A type of prameha characterised by sweet, sugarcane-like urine (glycosuria). An early or intermediate stage of diabetes where blood glucose appears in the urine. Requires blood-sugar regulating herbs.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Anti-diabetic; alleviating prameha group of diseases

diseases.description: The most severe type of prameha — characterised by honey-like sweet urine, excessive thirst, and progressive wasting. Corresponds to diabetes mellitus. In Ayurveda, the most difficult prameha to cure, often requiring lifelong management. Caused by depletion of ojas and vitiation of kapha, vāta.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Anti-diabetic; alleviating prameha group of diseases, esp. madhumeha

diseases.description: Chronic autoimmune skin disease with rapid skin cell proliferation causing thick silvery scales and red patches. In Ayurveda considered a type of mahā kuṣṭha (major skin disease) — eka kuṣṭha — caused by vitiated vāta, pitta, and kapha affecting the seven skin layers.

A wedge-shaped fleshy growth on the conjunctiva that can extend onto the cornea — associated with UV exposure and chronic irritation. In Ayurveda classified as a blood-tinged growth (raktārma) on the eye surface.

Disorders occurring in the post-partum period — including post-partum pain, fever, infection, retained lochia, and weakness. In Ayurveda the sūtikā (new mother) is considered vulnerable to vāta vitiation and requires specific dietary and herbal support for 42 days.
Specific post-partum pain including uterine cramping (afterpains) and musculoskeletal discomfort after delivery. Requires analgesic and vāta-pacifying herbs.

A classical Ayurvedic ritual and herbal treatment believed to influence the sex determination of the foetus. Described in detail in classical texts as a saṁskāra (ritual procedure) during early pregnancy.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Drugs which help getting male progeny; ritual measures for male progeny; reversal of sex of foetus during pregnancy

diseases.description: Therapeutic purgation — one of the five Panchakarma procedures. Used to eliminate excess pitta and kapha from the body through the lower GI tract. A fundamental purification therapy in Ayurveda, with three grades: mild (mṛdu), moderate (madhya), and drastic (tīkṣṇa).
See DIS-483 for complete entry. This ID reserved for database cross-reference alignment.
See DIS-449 for complete entry. This ID reserved for database alignment.

Rejuvenative therapy — one of the eight branches of Ayurveda. Rasāyana herbs and preparations promote longevity, retard ageing, enhance immunity, improve dhātu quality, and restore vitality. Used in healthy individuals for prevention and in the chronically ill for restoration.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Rasāyana (promotive therapy e.g. rejuvenation, restorative, alterative, protective); age-sustaining (vayaḥsthāpana), anti-aging etc.

diseases.description: See DIS-463 for complete entry. This ID reserved for database alignment.

Restoration of normal skin pigmentation after depigmentation conditions like vitiligo or leucoderma. In Ayurveda, repigmentation therapy involves herbs that stimulate melanocytes and restore normal tvak varṇa (skin colour).

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Producing paleness in skin (restoring normal colour)

diseases.description: Protrusion of the rectum through the anus. In Ayurveda a vāta disorder with weakening of the pelvic floor muscles and anal sphincter. Associated with chronic constipation, diarrhoea, and weakness.

Inability to urinate despite a full bladder. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated vāta obstructing the mūtravaha srotas. Can result from enlarged prostate, neurological conditions, or post-surgical complications.

Chronic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis affecting multiple joints symmetrically with morning stiffness, swelling, and progressive joint damage. In Ayurveda, āmavāta is caused by āma (undigested metabolic toxins) combining with vitiated vāta and lodging in joints. A distinct clinical entity described in detail in classical texts.

herbs.name: Pañcakola
herbs.botanical: Group: Pippali, Pippalimula, Cavya, Citraka, Sunthi

diseases.description: Fungal skin infection causing ring-shaped, itchy, scaly patches. In Ayurveda classified as a type of kṣudra kuṣṭha (minor skin disease) — dadru — caused by vitiated kapha and pitta affecting the outer skin layers.

Tuberculosis of the lymph nodes — particularly cervical lymph nodes forming a chain of nodular enlargements. In Ayurveda, apacī is a kapha-medas disease forming granthis (nodules) in the neck and body.

Enlargement of the scrotum — including hydrocele, varicocele, orchitis, and lymphatic filariasis of the scrotum. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated vāta, kapha, or all three doṣas accumulating in the vṛṣaṇa (testes) region.

Chronic sinus tract or fistula — a channel leading from a focus of infection to the body surface. Also includes chronic sinusitis. In Ayurveda, nāḍīvraṇa is a chronic suppurating channel caused by incompletely healed wounds or abscesses, requiring both wound-cleansing and wound-healing therapies.

General category for common skin disorders not falling under the specific kuṣṭha classification — including dermatitis, urticaria, rashes, and infectious skin conditions. Caused by vitiated doṣas affecting the multiple layers of skin (tvak).
Loss of firmness and tone of the breasts — occurring post-partum, with ageing, or after significant weight loss. In Ayurveda related to depletion of māṁsa and meda dhātus in the stana region.

A condition described in classical Ayurveda characterised by excessive whitening of the skin, excessive fluid secretion, and nutritional imbalance. Some scholars equate it with albinism or a specific type of anaemia with fluid disorders.

Enlargement of the spleen — can result from infections, haematological conditions, portal hypertension, or autoimmune diseases. In Ayurveda plīhā roga (spleen disease) involves vitiated pitta, kapha, and meda dhātu.
Treatment to stabilise an unstable or threatened foetus at risk of miscarriage. Herbs that pacify vāta, nourish the uterine lining, and support the developing foetus.

Inability to conceive after regular unprotected intercourse for one year. In Ayurveda caused by vitiation of śukra (semen) or ārtava (ovum), uterine disorders, or systemic weakness affecting the reproductive dhātus.

Inflammation of the mucous membranes of the mouth, causing painful ulcers, redness, and difficulty eating. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated pitta and rakta affecting the mukha region. Includes aphthous ulcers and infectious stomatitis.

Heat stroke — hyperthermia from excessive sun exposure causing headache, confusion, flushing, and loss of consciousness. In Ayurveda caused by excess pitta and increased body heat depleting ojas and body fluids.
Diseases above the clavicle — the Ayurvedic specialty of śālākya tantra (ENT and ophthalmology) covering head, neck, and sense organ diseases. General treatment for conditions in this region.
Allergic contact dermatitis or toxic swelling caused by exposure to bhallātaka (Semecarpus anacardium). A well-documented side-effect of marking-nut requiring specific antidote therapy.

Sexually transmitted bacterial infection (Treponema pallidum) causing primary ulcers, secondary rash, and potential tertiary systemic involvement. Phiraṅga in classical Ayurveda was a late-entering disease (possibly post-Columbian introduction) treated with specific anti-syphilitic herbs.

Loss of taste or abnormal taste perception. A common symptom accompanying fever, liver disorders, and digestive weakness. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated pitta affecting the rasanendriya (taste organ) or kapha coating the tongue.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Promoting desire for food and relish
Promoting desire for food and relish

diseases.description: Ringing, buzzing, or other noises in the ear without external stimulus. In Ayurveda a vāta disorder affecting the śrotraindriya — caused by vitiated vāta creating abnormal movements in the ear channels.

Inflammation and infection of the tonsils causing sore throat, difficulty swallowing, fever, and enlarged glands. In Ayurveda caused by vitiated kapha and pitta accumulating in the gala (throat) and tālū (palate) region.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Removing, pacifying, decreasing and alleviating kapha

diseases.description: Pain in or around a tooth — from cavities, exposed roots, cracked teeth, abscess, or gum disease. In Ayurveda a vāta or kapha condition of the dantakoṣa (dental socket) region.

Breaking of a tooth from trauma, grinding, or decay. Requires healing of surrounding tissue and prevention of secondary infection. In Ayurveda focuses on wound healing and strengthening the remaining dental structure.

Upward movement of vāta causing belching, hiccough, abdominal discomfort, and cardiac pain — when gas moves upward instead of downward. A vāta disorder of the gastrointestinal tract involving reversal of normal peristalsis.

associated_sanskrit_terms.meaning: Carminative; proper downward movement of vāta
